Stay Out Of The House has been in heavy development for years and now it's finally here.

The final product is filled with little treats of lore, a bunch of scares, and overall a very innovative game gameplay wise.

The first chapter is mostly waiting for things to happen but it stretches the tension out and actually makes you fearful. The ending scare was pretty good and truly got me.

The intro was really just introducing you to the main characters and the butcher.

On my first run of the house I started wandering the area, not sure of my objective. Suddenly I got spotted by the camera and the alarm went off. Which immediately got me killed. On the other two days I couldn't get anything done because I was too dumb to figure it out (plus I had not played the version in 2018) so I ended up dying.

But for my honest opinion, I loved the game. It was challenging yet possible, the visuals were beautiful yet still scary, and the butcher's AI was unpredictable. Overall this game deserves a 10/10 in my book.

Incredibly cool, scary, and immersive game. You can see that a lot of passion went into this title. These developers just love what they are doing. They understand the simplicity of what makes a game really scary.
If you like old-school graphics and 80s slasher movies, this is absolutely for you - in fact, every Puppet Combo game is.

This is a game that wholeheartedly embraces its retro roots with pixelated graphics that harken back to a bygone era of gaming. As you venture into its peculiar world, there is no denying the charm of its intentionally antiquated visuals. The pixelated art style manages to strike a delicate balance between nostalgia and creepiness, transporting you to a time when games were simpler, yet no less scary.

To head straight to the chopping block. This game is not your grandma's knitting club; it is a heart-pounding, gut-wrenching serial killer escape simulator. Your job, should you choose to accept it, is to escape that house of horrors by any means necessary. 

Hang on to your apron strings; it is not all fun and games. You will taste the consequences of The Butcher's culinary skills firsthand. It is a bad cooking show: a swing of the hammer, a loud thud, and you are upstairs, locked in a cage.

There are moments of genuine confusion that add an extra layer of challenge and intrigue. It can be a bit akin to deciphering an ancient cryptic puzzle—thrilling, occasionally leaving you scratching your head and wondering, "What in the haunted world am I supposed to do here?" This nature keeps you on your toes, never knowing what absurdity or fright awaits you next.

In this freaky-deaky house, silence is golden, and stealth is your bestie. The Butcher has ears like a hawk and can hear you rummaging for snacks from miles away. You will stumble upon tools and items in this digital madhouse that will make your escape dreams a reality. Your brainpower will be your greatest asset as you navigate this puzzle-infested labyrinth.

Any encounter with the game's bizarre cast of characters is a warped trip down memory lane. It is a dysfunctional family reunion. The pixelated visuals blur the line between familiar and freaky. The visuals contribute to the game's twisted charm.

It may be confusing at times, though it is precisely this confusion that adds to the game's allure. You have to piece together a puzzle without a guide; that challenge is part of the fun. It pushes you to think outside the box, to explore every nook and cranny, and to unravel the mysteries hidden within every corridor.

Stay Out of The House (SOOTH) is a fantastic indie horror game held back by its own bugs and technical faults. The game develops and expands in novel ways where logic and survival are paramount; in ways which are interesting and generally intelligent. The game has a fun PS1 style aesthetic to it, with a Grindhouse design to follow. Fundamentally, it has similar beats to that of a Chilla's Art game (Convenience Store), with a much more developed and enjoyable gameplay loop to that of the Granny horror game series. Sprinkle in some Chainsaw Massacre and Silent Hill, and you have this wonderful mess of a project. The rub is that SOOTH - despite being in development for over 4 years - still has game impacting bugs. This could be anywhere from certain items not working (hex key unable to open some locks despite having spare paperclips, the gun not reloading despite having bullets, and the screen effects triggering and remaining even after a set amount of time has passed) each of which require a reset; In a game which has a set number of allocated saves. These issues may arguably play into this nostalgic design, but they're the issues which should have been left behind and fixed. Other bugs and AI features are less glaring, but I can't help but wonder what is intentional and/or a byproduct of this chaotic game's ethos: for example some sounds in this game can be excruciatingly annoying to hear. All in all, I love this game. I think it's one of Puppet Combo's best works, and that it's a beautiful cultivation of all their previous projects. It's terrifying, frustrating, and captivating in all the best ways. It just needs some more time in the stew, assuming it's not intentionally meant to be this raw.

Review: Stay Out of the House is a proper horror game that seeks to use your own fears against you, all the while requiring that you focus on logic, and reason to get through specific conundrums. This game is highly recommended because it invoked in me a primal sort of anxiety that few games seem to be able to reach in my dopamine/serotonin deficient brain. The whole presentation is like some strange fever-dream that gets into your head in strange ways. There is a suspension of disbelief brought about by the strong plot, the memorable characters, and the overall atmosphere/aesthetics in general.

Visuals: The graphics are intentionally created in such a way as to emulate the look of PS1, and early DOS based 3d polygonal games circa 1995-1998. 

Audio: Creepy, and appropriate. There are times when the sound (or lack thereof) creates a crescendo of atmospheric fear.

Overall rating: 10/10 from a veteran gamer that started with floppy disk games back in the late 80's.

A sneaky spooky game where you crouch around the house of a deranged serial killer. There’s a lot of these games out there. Stealth games set in confined spaces, where you need to avoid the gaze of a roaming monster as you look for keys and unlock doors.

Stay Out of The House is a little more systemic in its approach. There are consequences as you play. Instead of immediately throwing you back to the main menu, the killer keeps tally as he locks you up again. As you break out, new security measures are in place. Surveillance cameras. Traps littering the floors and rooms. Even where you previously explored.

Got caught hiding under a bed? That bed is flipped now -- permanently. Even the old reliable air ducts that snake around the house aren’t safe.

So there’s a pretty cool economy going on here, punishing you for doing badly by making things even worse. It’s a very thematic detail that fits the rest of the aesthetics perfectly.

Recommended if you enjoy spooky PS1 graphics and punishing, somewhat janky, gameplay.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

It is definitely not another horror walking-sim, it has much more depth than you might think. Although it is "just" an indie game, Resident Evil 7 feels lame in comparison to this masterpiece.

For those who bought it - do yourself a favor and try to get all endings, as there is more than one layer of the story in this game (and each is satisfying).

A survival horror taking some inspiration from The Texas Chainsaw Massacre.

The game is split into four sections that you can start from the main menu. The first has you playing as a woman arriving to work at a gas station who goes through a night of work doing things like sweeping and playing the Power Drill Massacre arcade machine before being attacked and captured by a masked killer. The second section of the game has you playing as the main character riding in a car with her boyfriend until he stops for a bathroom break and disappears. Attempting to find him you walk through a cornfield and find a seemingly abandoned home before being captures by the same masked man.

The third section is where the majority of the game takes place with you waking up in a cage facing a TV you can't shut off. From there you need to escape the cage, sneak around the house avoiding the masked man who is in the process of cutting up some of his latest victims, discover notes and items that can reveal more information on the settings backstory, locate items needed to disable traps to find the key to exit the house while possibly leading other survivors to a safe room. Your biggest obstacle is likely to be your inventory size, unless you can find the backpack, with you needing to make use of wire cutters, screwdrivers, a lighter, video tapes acts like a Resident Evil ink ribbon, lockpicks, keys, etc to advance to new areas of the house while defensive items like a revolver and knife can drive away the killer temporarily. Items can be dropped anywhere though so it is more deciding what you need and want rather than having to run to a designated storage spot to swap items out. Some passive items can be found that don't take up inventory space like a flashlight that takes the place of your lighter as a source of light, a backpack to double your inventory, and a device that shows you the level of light you are standing in. You can run and jump but staying quiet and in the darker areas of the house while leaving lights off is often your best bet as the killer tends to keep a set movement schedule around the house unless he sees or hears you. What can lead to further difficulties is the grandma in a wheelchair who starts moving around the house and screams when she sees you and a baby that crawls through the vents that often act as a save place and access to your save point who might run from or attempt to bite you. Reloading games or killing the grandma can have the killer setting alarm tripwires and bear traps around the house, turning on lights, and locking doors. Over time the killer will go out into the backyard where other victims are kept caged up and kill them, freeing them and leading them to your save room will give you some dialogue for both plot and hints of what to do. On the hardest difficulty injuries need to be healed with health items to avoid bleeding out and food needs to be eaten to manage hunger.

Escaping from the house leads to one of the game's endings but finding a secret route into the bunker opens the fourth section of the game that leads to new endings and information on what is happening in the house.

There are some cool features most people won't think about in the game like being able to bypass a lot of the locked doors by damaging the lock with a bullet or melee weapon and secret areas you can enter by jumping on furniture and climbing into vents. You have a variety of visual options with a CRT effect toggle and changing settings to make it look like it was shot on a bad mid or late 90s video camera.

Solid horror title that can start to become easy to predict as you go back and forth to manage inventory and look for puzzle solutions but also has some good interactions, rewarding small victories, and good atmosphere.

TLDR: Stressful, confusing, and a bit janky at times, but still a solid survival horror. Big rec if you're a fan of Puppet Combo or wanted something in the vain of Alien Isolation, but in a PSX style.

Pros: Spooky Atmosphere the whole way through. The first two parts of the game do it best, but the 3rd part is still really tense. It just loses out that spookiness a bit in place of stress since The Butcher never leaves you alone. It feels rewarding getting through a lot of the puzzles and finding the few save rooms in this game. The sound design is also good. You feel very tense hearing the butcher or various other things in the game getting near you. The story and lore is also interesting. Would've thought it'd just be cheesy B-Slasher stuff, but it's that and a bit more. There's also more depth to the gameplay then you would think. Didn't know [spoiler] you can use the gun to shoot doorknobs off or that you can get the butcher to step on his own traps, [/spoiler]. You have to manually load the gun and sometimes pick locks in the heat of things, so that adds on to the tenseness. Solid stuff overall.

Cons: During the house phase the butcher chasing you everywhere makes sense, but during [spoiler] the bunker phase [/spoiler], him being everywhere becomes way too annoying. You just want like 5 minutes to go through puzzles read the notes or explore, but you can't really do that when you hear *thump thump* every 30 seconds. The puzzles feel good to solve, but a lot of them feel very vague in HOW to solve them. I felt like I explored every room in the game like 100 times since I didn't know what to do sometimes. Item management is also an issue. You'll pick up a lot of items, but not have enough room for them (even when you get the backpack increase). There's no storage box like in RE, so you just have to drop everything and remember where you left it.

Glitches: Encountered a few, like granny not being able to detect me even when I'm staring at her in the face, the radar not working half the time, items being stuck inside of wardrobes. Almost forgot, but I was putting the batteries in the can opener, saved the game and quit, and after the update on 10/21, the batteries where just all gone when I loaded the game.. Nothing game breaking (for me at least), but still glitches. 

I really liked it overall, despite how annoyed I got throughout it. Been waiting some time for it to come out and I think it delivered. I just think it could still use some QOL updates, like either more inventory or a storage box, maybe some more notes explaining what the hell you're supposed to do (not so much that it holds your hand the whole time, but enough to know what to do), have the butcher chill out a bit and not show up like every few seconds later on in the game, and fixing some of the glitches. Losing your items every time you die is also wack, since after a few times of that happening it makes you want to reload your save. Don't know if this was changed after the update on 10/21 since when I died, my items were all around me, but if it's still there, would rather it be gone lol.

As a long time fan, I've definitely been interested in his projects for a long ass time over the years, and SOOTH has been in development hell for a long ass time, so finally seeing it release in a...Decent state is nice.

Basically? It's inspired by Granny, and aims to give an experience of that game but actually good :^) (i'd also say Hello Neighbor to an extent? Similar concept, but Granny might've had inspirations from that...Oh also SOOTH isn't a fucking shitfest like Hello Neighbor, or a snoozefest like Granny.)

So, the game has you sneaking around a creepy house while solving puzzles and avoiding the Butcher's crazy ass family. While along the way learning how to deal with the various threats and traps you'll encounter
(Such as finding a way to safely disable the security cameras instead of loudly shooting them with your revolver, for example)

With that being said, I genuinely think SOOTH is a GREAT fuckin' horror game, probably one of my favorites, but it does have some glaring issues.

I think the release was rushed even with the multiple delays, there's a lot of bugs present - especially with the save system introduced in the launch.

Basically? Saving seems to not remember a whole lot of things in the game, this includes:
*Some events (like the vent at the beginning with the prompt to "look" through them will appear again when reloading your save.)
*Weather or not doors are locked (the doors will remain unlocked, however the locks will be reset and you'll have a prompt to unlock them regardless.)
*I'd assume beds that are flipped over by the Night Shift Abductor reset back to normal as well
*Security cameras being brought back to life, rather frustratingly.
*Some other tomfoolery I likely haven't found yet, likely relating to the other endings.

There are other bugs and little polish inconsistencies as well.
A few examples would be...

The prompt to crawl through the fan within the vents next to the safehouse doesn't show up when going back the other way, so it's basically a one-way-trip which is rather frustrating (especially since you COULD go back in Nun Massacare)

Some lighting issues and cracks in the geometry (light peeking through the vents in the area where you first find the Butcher chopping up meat after getting the screwdriver and entering the vents.
The other big one would be where you find Brendan, when exiting the vents you can see that the walls aren't high enough, and you can see into different rooms - it looks extremely sloppy.)

Being in the vents muffles all of the sound as well, so you can't hear the Grandma's loud ass electric chair thing, or the Butcher's footsteps too. Which makes exiting the vents at good times difficult.

There might also be issues with the security cameras noticing you, I've had plenty of instances where I was in the line of sight with them, only for them to not go off. Ontop of the light having a tendency to clip through walls (you also can't be spotted when in a vent by the security cameras.)

I REALLY wish you would add a button to holster your currently held item as well! If possible in the future, same with adding a button to hide the stealth light meter.


With those out of the way, I'm REALLY hoping they get patched in a future update, as they take a massive hit to the game's experience as a whole, but even with that in mind I can still 100% reccomend picking it up if you're a fan of stealth horror games. I'd just suggest not saving for the time being for the best experience.


Regardless, I'm super excited to see how PDM will go for you in the future, you've honestly become one of my favorite horror game devs in general, Combo. So definitely keep up the good work, here's hoping you get these bugs ironed out too.

Stay Out of the House delivers an intense, old-school survival horror experience that had me on the edge of my seat. As the protagonist trapped overnight in a sinister house, you have to carefully explore creepy rooms trying to find keys and tools to make your escape.

The retro PS1-style visuals are effectively lo-fi - the pixelated graphics and muddy color palette create an unsettling atmosphere right from the start. The house feels distinctly eerie and lived-in thanks to little environmental details. Flickering lights and strange noises had me dreading every room I entered.

Your only defense against the disturbing creatures roaming the halls are some basic tools like planks and knives. Combat is purposely clunky and frantic, making every encounter scarily desperate. Hiding or running tend to be smarter than fighting.

Puzzles require you to pay close attention to clues and patterns, creating rewarding "aha!" moments when you figure them out. Solving puzzles unlocks new rooms and items key for progressing the maze-like house.

With no hand holding, I often felt disoriented and anxious in the best way. The lack of guidance and unpredictable enemy patterns challenged me to think on my feet. Death was frequent but checkpoints were fairly forgiving.

Occasional technical issues like frame rate dips happened, but nothing too bothersome. The chilling ambient soundtrack and unnerving sound effects completed the frightening atmosphere.

For only $14.99 , Stay Out of the House succeeds as a short, fierce horror game. The retro aesthetic and intense survival gameplay recaptured the PS1 era's experimental, haunting feel. This is a must-play for old-school survival horror fans. Just be prepared for an uncomfortable night!

Welcome to Mill Creek, a small town in Oklahoma with a big problem. There is a “Midnight Abductor” snatching up people and bringing them to his house for unknown purposes. For the prelude to this game, you get a firsthand account of being abducted as one of his victims. That whole set up was masterfully crafted with the developer building tension and anxiety! In the main game you are his latest victim, and you will soon find out what he has in store for you. If you want to survive, your best bet is to escape the house. The house is worn down and heavily inspired by The Texas Chainsaw Massacre. You will find everyday household items such as lamp shades made from human flesh, light bulbs made of severed heads, and human rugs. Super creepy, macabre, and great atmosphere. 

As you are trying to find a way to escape the house, the Midnight Abductor (also known as The Butcher), will try to thwart your efforts. He has bear traps scattered around, cameras, and other means to ferret out where you are. You on the other hand are not defenseless and can fight back by disabling his traps, use them against him, and fend him off temporarily with weapons. Navigate the house through an interconnected ventilation system, allowing you to bypass traps or escape the butcher’s clutches. Don’t expect the vents to be 100% safe though.

What makes the stalker in this game unique is the tit for tat nature he exhibits, which is more align to a human with rational thinking than something animalistic in nature. The darkness is your friend as it allows you to skulk about unseen. The Butcher, knowing this, periodically turns on lights as he searches for you, making your job harder. If you make a loud noise and hide, he will search for you. Upon not finding you, he will place a bear trap to assist with ensnaring you. You can find a radar and use it to track The Butcher, however, sometimes he will stand still potentially catching you off guard if you bump into him.

The biggest critiques I have are as follows. As you pick up new items and use them, sometimes the items in your inventory will change location. So, I may be trying to pull out the revolver and find out its inventory slot has changed. This is easily the best Puppet Combo game and one of the best indie horror games out there. It's also one of the biggest indie horror games I've seen but it has some major flaws. 

The gameplay is very similar to Granny but expanded greatly with more gameplay elements, story, etc. You get 3 tries (except there are RE style saves, so you won't lose all progress) to escape a killer's house. You find items around the house and you have to figure out where to use them while avoiding the killer by hiding in the darkness, crawling through vents, or even fighting back. It's tense, it's scary, and you'll probably not make it out alive.

[i] Pros [/i]
-2 pretty big and interconnected maps with tons to explore and doors to unlock
-great spooky atmosphere
-great ps1 low poly graphics
-the story is pretty good, it's fun to find things and slowly piece together all the details
-is actually scary and doesn't really rely on loud jumpscares (they are in the game but they are the main focus)
-The layout of the house and bunker is very well made, there's tons of paths, secrets, etc.
-Multiple endings
-good sound design
-Closing Shift is great and it is pretty much it's own little horror game
-photo mode (although bugged currently and haven't got to check it out)

[i] Cons [/i]  
-Bugs. The game is filled with bugs, Most are smaller things like (the killer walking through things, dead people coming back to life after save, etc.) but some can ruin your run, forcing you to load your last save. The devs are working hard on fixing some of the bigger ones but many still remain.
-Sometimes it's really hard to hear the killer's footsteps, leading to him seeing you even though you couldn't see or hear him at all.
-It can be a little difficult to figure out what you are meant to do without watching a tutorial at times

Even with it's problems, if you like horror games in the slightest, you need to try this game out. It is a really well made indie horror game with quite a lot of content. I highly recommend it.

I was REALLY enjoying playing this game. The first two parts of the game were spooky, suspenseful, and incredibly fun. Once I got to part three (the house), the game switches gears, and you begin to solve puzzles, and try and figure out how to escape your captor. All of that sounds good on paper, except as it stands right now, the game is incredibly unbalanced, and unfair.

The Butcher or his Grandma are always nearby. Not the biggest issue, since this is a stealth game. However, if I successfully pick a lock, I'm immobilized as the cabinet begins the slow animation of opening, and right on cue, the screen starts to emit static--indicating that the Butcher is nearby--and my death is all but assured. Some areas are safer than others. When I'm not crawling through the vents, I spend a lot of my time in dark rooms. I listen for the footsteps/scooter noise to trail off, and then when I assume all is clear, I try to solve a puzzle, or proceed in the next room, only for the Butcher to pop around the corner and bust my head in. The game slowly transitioned from fun and terrifying, to frustrating and upsetting. I haven't been able to make any progress past where I am, and I've gotten the revolver.

Speaking of, if i'm lucky enough to get some shots off (big if) the majority of the time I engage with the Butcher, I'm immobilized on first hit. Has anyone else experienced this?! Not that I guess it matters much if I could move, since most of the screen goes red, and fills with static, and my sense of direction is thrown out the window.

You get three chances (days) in the house if you die, though honestly, you might as well reset if you do, since you lose all of your items, and have to spend the majority of your time recollecting them again. None of this would be an issue, if I could save the game more often. I've scoured the house, and have found two video tapes, which let you save your progress. When should you use them? Hell, if I know. No matter when you do, you're going to be redoing a lot of what you did before anyway.

You're locked in a big house with a maniac and you have to find a way out but you have only 3 days (3 lives) to find tools, keys and items to protect yourself and progress through the game. Many dangers in the house but also many ways to solve the problems, for example it's nice to see that you have several ways to deactivate the cameras in the house. You ask yourself "oh does the game allows me to do this?" and here you go, it does! The game isn't just "find the right item to use at the right place, it respects the basic logic the player will have when he's facing a problem and it brings a lot of self confidence to move further into the house despite this very stressful feeling of constant danger and the overwhelming difficulty (at least during the first hour). You want to explore, to disable the traps, to go beyond these locked doors, to kill that awful grandma!

I was disappointed by quite a few indie horror games because of sometimes a gameplay too simple with a lack of challenge, sometimes a slow pace (too slow) but this game really delivered. This is one of the best horror games ever made, and easily my pick for Game of the Year 2022. If you've been looking for a Granny-like game with a smart killer, tense atmosphere, challenging and interesting puzzles, and LOTS of scares, this is it.

There's a ton of content for the asking price and plenty of replay value, thanks to immersive sim elements and secrets giving you a myriad of unique ways to progress towards the same goal. Accessing a new area might require solving multiple puzzles to get around a locked door... or perhaps you could swipe a key from the killer's back pocket and use it to get through the door early, or maybe you'll have some bullets to spare and feel like shooting the door open... this is just an example of some of the complex gameplay this game lends itself to.

Compared to the early access version, the full release adds a brand new chapter to the game that doubles the total content and playtime, if you're interested in getting the best ending. In terms of quality, the new content is superb, and gives you even more of the same puzzling & stealth gameplay the rest of the game already does so well.

Lastly, the game rests on a surprisingly complex enemy AI, which really escalates the gameplay and tension. If you were disappointed by the failure of Hello Neighbor (advertised as an AI sandbox, despite actual gameplay making the enemy almost helpless to navigate his own house), you might find something great in this one. At times, playing against the killer really feels like trying to outsmart another human being, that's trying to predict your moves before you make them. It's extremely refreshing to learn his habits and think of counterplay as you go.

This review has likely gone on for long enough. If all of the above sounds interesting to you, get this game and don't look back. Ever. Seriously, you will not regret it. It's awesome.

Amazing game. Playing with headphones is horrifying and I will never forget my first playthrough of this game for how scared it made me. The stealth aspect is done really well, the butcher and grandma both have mostly unpredictable AI and staying hidden from them can be challenging and exhilarating. While I think the game is great, there are a few points that I have issues with. 1. Towards the beginning of the game there is little to no save points. It's very hard to find more save items until after you've completed a puzzle or two which is pretty hard with both grandma and the butcher and the small size of the house at the beginning. 2. Some of the puzzle solutions- well, two in particular- are extremely hard and require way to much exploration and backtracking for a single puzzle each. Not going to say which ones, but if you find yourself scratching your head for a good bit, it's probably the one you're on. 3. there is no "good" ending. there are multiple endings, but each of them are bad in their own way. I get what the purpose behind each ending was, but I still wish the protagonist could get a happy end with all the victims you save along the way. speaking of victims, 4. Saving the victims is usually not beneficial or rewarding. Since there's no "good" ending where you escape with all the victims you rescued, saving them seems pointless on repeat playthroughs. For a first playthrough I would highly recommend it though, especially if you are stuck on a puzzle. There are two victims in particular that give hints for puzzles (one of which being one of the extremely hard ones, in fact the victims info is downright VITAL) so it's definitely a good idea to save them. From what I remember, the other two victims just give lore clues, which is nice also. Overall I loved this game, it is SO CLOSE to being perfect.

The game is also very repayable with the addition of the bunker which basically gives you different tasks to do and gives you a whole different experience which also gives the game so much more depth.

I have to say, the start of the game is incredibly boring. I understand these games need suspenseful intros and granted - when it hit me, it hit me GOOD. However me having to wait around just standing there and doing nothing for 30-35 minutes just for the intro just felt ridiculous. But hey, maybe I was the problem? I just feel like I did my objectives fairly quickly and was then forced to literally just stand around and be useless. There is an Arcade that you can play but that got old for me after 3 deaths.
Perhaps it's a way for the devs to stop people from refunding the game early? Whatever it is, sucks that this is the way it is.

With all that said, I have to admit Stay Out of the House must be my favourite entry from Puppet Combo games, in all seriouseness. Additional points for this game not relaying heavily on just ear-blasting screaming, and while yes - there is a little of that, it uh - can be *helped* I guess you could say, AND the devs graciously offered us a specific slider in the audio settings dedicated to screamers. Love to see that, because that's number 1 reason why I often have a hard time enjoying Puppet Combo's games, if they insist on making you go deaf before the age of 30 because, you know - loud = scary.
In all seriouseness though, the scariest sh*t in this game is when you're focused on doing something, like aiming your screwdriver into a screw obscured by the horrible lighting, hands shaking as you hear steps in the distance slowly approaching, closer and closer, and you try to greed it a little bit because I mean SURELY you can make it... And the steps suddenly come much closer and much quicker, and in a second you're getting your ribs rearranged. Lack of any music here other than the sound ques is absolutely terrifying.

Puzzles here are pretty straight forward, but there is a lot to do, and it's a good thing. The layout of the house is fun in that regard and you're never really lost. Though toward the end of the game I did get stuck for literally an hour, but turns out that to put it simply - gamers never look up xd

Lastly, I LOVE the setting for this game! A young woman kidnapped and held prisoner in a farm. Makes you feel naked and vulnerable. The killer himself gives me a vibe of a beautiful mix of Leatherface from Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Jason Voorhees from Friday the 13th Part 2, absolutely perfect combo in my opinion! 
I also have to mention the AI is actually really fun to go against here. The Butcher has a routine, he walks around doing his thing, going back and forth, grabbing more meat and chopping. There's things you can do in the world that will make him get angry. He's a relentless hunter but it is also possible to run away from him. You can try hiding in the vents, but if he notices you - he will run and try to lure you out. He can also sometimes sneak up on you very well. All this makes him feel very genuine, like it's not an artificial difficulty, or a scripted one. Very much enjoyed that!

Also, before I finish this off - I would love for Puppet Combo to ditch the save system. I feel it's pretty useless, because, for me personally anyway - whenever I would get caught I would simply load the game. Yes, the saves are limited, but there's easily more than enough for you to save every now and then whenever you make some amount of progress. Ditch this mechanic, and instead maybe give us a variety of possible death animations, you know - a little more something like Granny had (and to clarify, I'm not a big fan of Granny but admittedly that game can stand it's own ground, I just thought that part of Granny would fit here a lot better than what we have). Keep the mechanic where getting caught means waking up in a different room, with a different puzzle, each time getting you closer to actual death - I feel like that would be just perfect.
Of course, I'm not expecting for this to suddenly become a reality after so much time has passed, but if not that, then at least maybe for the future? ;) 
Besides, a man can dream :P

In conclusion - the start of the game sucks wrinkly balls, but the rest of the game is absolutely amazing!

Stay Out of the House does a lot of things that normally might be considered too tedious for modern games, but all of it feels completely necessary and improves the experience. You can't use save states or save often, instead you'll need to scavenge the house for VHS tapes and carry them to the one save room, and each of these saves are single-use. This is one of the few horror games I've played to genuinely scare me and inflict dread that I can remember. The game takes its time building suspense (arguably too much in the prologue), making you dread what is going to happen next, then it hits you with a gut punch jumpscare that feels earned and makes you jump in your seat and panic. The core game after the lengthy prologue is one of very few horror games whose scares feel natural, that how you played resulted in proper consequences. Its initially limited inventory places emphasis on item management much like classic resident evil and more recently Signalis (which I also highly recommend!), which drives the tension extremely high. Many of the items you acquire can be used in a surprising number of ways, almost to the level of an immersive sim at times. The limited saves also create a very intense dread when you've been too greedy with the video tapes. The 3-day system is somewhat strange to me and I mostly ignored it (except in one instance, if you've played you probably know), opting instead to reload my save whenever I died. I imagine you could do a semi-challenge run trying to beat the game without reloading saves and only using the 3-life system, but all-in-all its just a strange addition that I did not know how to integrate into play. I do like the randomization of your items in the house and placing you in new strange sections of the house (especially when you are still familiarizing yourself with its layout), however that system alongside the save system just seem a bit incongruent to me, though it hardly detracts from the quality of the game. All of the endings are fun to get, and how they interop with the story is fun. The story itself is fine, it mostly takes a backseat, but the bunker expands on it somewhat which feels nice. Nothing amazing but it provides the game with good flavor. The AI of the killer is top-notch and surprised me many times. The layout/level design of the house is awesome, always hiding away secret nooks and rooms, making it feel as though the house is expanding and swallowing you whole. Once you think you know the layout, you find an entirely new area that interlinks with places past and you have to learn the whole thing all over again, it is wonderful to navigate. The stealth mechanics are great, using light and sound effectively (although I found the sound meter to be mostly obsolete, you can usually tell how much sound you're making well). I also love the clunky reload of the revolver; if you spend too much ammo and miss too much, you're forced into a long panicked reload, though this only happened a couple times in my playthrough (somewhat wish ammo was just slightly more scarce, though I was super thorough unlocking all the locked drawers and cabinets I could). The game's PSX/retro visuals are decent, they get the job done and leave a lot of room for interpretation, adding to the horror of it all. The sound design is also amazing, the sounds of the killer, fumbling over physics props that make noise and give away your location, Granny, etc. On an input level, the game fumbles a bit I think, it could've allowed for at least one more input to differentiate using the item in your hand from interacting with something in the world; it sucks to fumble through your randomly changing inventory slots to try and close a door quickly and you end up shooting your gun for example.

All-in-all, I got a solid 18 hours of some of the best horror in a game I've experienced. And at the price point its at, this game is a steal.

9/10 !! I'll preface this by saying I've never written a review before, let alone one this long. Fair warning for that. 

Stay Out of The House is a love letter to the classic horror genre, and its influences: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Hills Have Eyes. I've been following the development of this game since 2019, along with puppet combo's other growing titles. I'm happy to have seen the progression of puppet combo as a developer and the cult following that they've (rightfully) garnered.

Sooth is a game I've been waiting a long time for, so I wanted to make sure to leave an in depth review that'd inform others of what a great game experience it is, gratitude for the developer's creativity, and leave my appreciation for it in other regards aside from the gameplay elements.

Its visual style is one of the most dinghy, sleazy, crunchy, and uncanny that I've seen in a game. There's a coat of grime all over this one, and I love it! With that being said, there's also an air of mystique and a dream-like surreal atmosphere to the world, feeling so vast yet congested and confined. I really appreciate that about puppet combo games, especially within the earlier era. This title and their others have proven to subvert the forceful and loud nature of the slasher genre and transform it into something quiet, and always leave the player with a feeling of anticipation. The unique stylistic choices combined with such a quiet atmosphere are what gives this game in particular the special edge compared to many modern horror game titles of our time. Subtlety is what really drove me to get invested in sooth initially. There’s a sense of emptiness, loneliness, and disconnect from you and your surroundings along with the nagging anxiety around the horrific imagery that seems to be lurking underneath the mundane. Puppet combo has a way of framing familiar surroundings and things you'd see normally and having them make you feel utterly confused and lost (I mean that in the best way.)

With that all being said, I'd like to actually talk about the gameplay now and criticisms I have.
I absolutely don't hate the lore aspects of this game, in fact, they're extremely compelling and the details left up for the player to discover and speculate were what deepened my interest in it! However, I can't help but be a bit disappointed when it comes to where the lore of the game stands now, along with the story direction other newer titles have been taking. (This will be spoiler free!)
I mentioned earlier that sooth along with the other puppet combo titles were subversive of the slasher and b grade movie genre, leaving much up to the imagination, being ambiguous and quiet. However, I feel that the recent plot directions have leaned a bit heavier into the b slasher horror genre, and are a bit excessive when it comes to the presentation of horror.  Not that the game, or other puppet combo titles aren't scary anymore, but I find that the effect has diminished with focusing more on the danger aspects in the gameplay and excessive tropes from those films (that being the use/execution of the traps, the victims around the house, and relying on more cheap scares rather than slower pacing.) Another issue I have is with the story of these games leaving little to the imagination, and over explaining the lore a bit. I noticed an overarching theme/force in the puppet combo world lore, and was glad that it was being further explored in the final release of sooth. However, it falls somewhat short in its execution: too many angles or concepts were explored in one sitting rather than leaving room for them to be processed or fester a bit, a considerable buildup. The plot would have benefited from slower pacing. Again, all of the concepts are very compelling in their own right, but it felt a bit anticlimactic to have the answers handed to us.

Critique out of the way, I am so thankful for the gameplay mechanics being polished, as it was one of the sole things this game was lacking in earlier builds. The use of the items, menu systems, and mechanics are tight, and work so much better. It's made the experience a lot more seamless. However, there are still a lot of glitches in this game. Thankfully they're mostly funny, like things clipping through the floor, butcher getting stuck and things floating. Other times they can be frustrating and hurt the experience, though. An entire shelf got stuck in a cabinet and a key item fell through the world, which was a bit much.  
The AI has been vastly improved and that aspect has enhanced the horror in this game: The butcher becomes aware of your patterns and corrects his past mistakes. It adds so much tension and higher stakes.

Overall, I would 100 percent recommend this game to every horror fan. I wouldn't be so in depth about my critique if I didn't appreciate these games so much and see the huge potential in them!

I played this game about a year ago and I ended up liking it quite a lot. To my surprise the game was very similar to one of Puppet Combo's previous games, Nun Massacre, where you're similarly stuck in a building, having to solve a series of puzzles to escape, while simultaneously trying to avoid and outsmart a relentless killer. To do this, the game offers a wide variety of survival tools which are progressively discovered throughout the game. These tools can range from traps, distractions, and even devices which can remove certain threats entirely.

The game offers absolutely zero handholding, which leaves it up to the player to experiment and figure things out for themselves, which also means a lot of the game consists of trial and error. This is something I personally enjoy a lot, especially in horror games. 

Despite staying in the same house for almost the entire game, there's a surprising level of depth to the exploration. Even after I thought I had seen everything, the house kept opening up in complex and interesting ways.

There's also a strong sense of personality and humor, like for example how the killer forces his victims watch brainwashing propaganda channels on the TVs scattered throughout the house, or how the Grandma can ride her wheelchair up and down a flight of stairs.

I unfortunately encountered a series of game breaking bugs during my playthrough, one of which ended up softlocking the game due to an item necessary for progression not spawning. However, due to most of the progression being knowledge based, replaying doesn't take very long.

Even a year later, I feel like I didn't give this nearly game enough credit, despite having overwhelmingly fond memories with it. I think Stay Out of the House is Puppet Combo's best yet. To me, their iconic style has always consisted of first-person survival-horror games with emphasis on environmental storytelling, puzzle solving, and difficulty. Games like Power Drill Massacre, Nun Massacre, and now finally, this game, Stay Out of the House. I heavily prefer these kinds of games compared to Puppet Combo's more story-oriented horror games, like Murder House, where the cheesy voice acting and scripted sequences typically ends up souring my experience.

As a major fan of Puppet Combo. I have to say that I found this game very impressive. Ever since the full release, there has been a few noticeable bugs in the game. But ever since the release, the developers had been trying their best to make some quality changes and patch out the bugs. They have even added a mechanic where you can actually use the hammer as a weapon! The only bugs I've found (at least from what I'm aware of) are when your FOV resets to default whenever the butcher steps on a bear trap and a bug where some of the doors are a bit flimsy. If you push a door even a little bit (like a love tap kind of push), the door would not stop moving until it reaches the wall. That bug specifically does terrify me because I do tend to worry that the butcher would just look around the corner and see me because I have the door WIDE open. But aside from those two bugs, that stuff could easily be overlooked in my opinion.

This game is really immersive. The sounds make the game suspenseful. The PS1-styled graphics makes the game feel nostalgic and gives you the feeling you are actually a character in an 80's slasher film. And the gameplay is just amazing. When you play this game, you have to be extremely careful about your actions depending on what difficulty your playing on. And that just perfectly captures what a horror game SHOULD BE. I would overall give this game a 9.5/10. The five or six years on this particular Puppet Combo game was indeed worth the wait for the full release. I would definitely recommend that more people would play their games.

Not gonna lie when I saw this game in development I was eager to play it- as I really loved Murder House and would consider it to be one of my favorite horror games.

Though this...unfortunately did not strike the same chord that Murder House did. Murder House was filled to the brim with atmosphere. Every level had music which not only built tension but made the world feel real and alive. The sounds, the ambience, the attention to detail in the maps themselves- it was a really well thought-out horror game.

While I see the potential in this game, it feels...unfinished. The first chapter in the gas station was incredibly boring. No sounds (and the sounds that do play are incredibly loud and have no distance meaning a customer could walk in and the door being extremely loud despite being on the other side of the store), no cheesy music in the background, nothing to immerse me in the experience. The doors in the game feel really lazy as well. On Murder House when you approach a door, it has that classic door opening animation from Resident Evil which really added to the suspension of what's on the other side. On here the doors just rely on physics and because of that I found myself getting stuck on them or not knowing how to properly open them.

After the gas station segment you're left at a parking lot with no clear direction on where to go. Yet again, no music or anything to make the atmosphere feel tense. I made it to the corn maze but honestly I was so underwhelmed that I really didn't feel like playing it anymore.

I'm sure I missed out on a big chunk of the game (y'know, the whole house with a cannibal killer), but if there's hardly any immersion put into the first few segments I have little to no reason to see what comes next.

Maybe I'll come back to this game but for now, I'd recommend just playing Murder House.

The game starts out as genuinely fairly creepy in act one, though I really wasn't a fan of how long it took for progression triggers to occur. I also had trouble working out where to put some of the items back where they belonged, but that could just be a me thing.

The second act was also frustrating. Like act one, it started out with a great vibe and atmosphere, but it quickly turned into frustration as I had a lot of trouble finding the TINY path in the wheat field behind the red ute. It took me 20 minutes to find that opening, and I only did so after hugging the wall. It was reeeally hard to see. After that it was smooth again and the atmosphere came back.

Act 3 is where I gave up. I understood what the game was trying to accomplish. It's clearly trying to take the first part of RE7 and turn it into a whole ass game, and that's a fantastic concept. But man... I can't help but feel like either my game is bugged or I was doing something wrong. I'll list my issues in dot points:

-Granny's wheelchair makes.. NO noise. At all. I don't know if this is intentional but I got caught by her constantly because she'd sneak up on me.
-An addendum to granny, she's also REALLY FAST. I also don't know if this is intentional but combined with the sheer silence of her wheelcheer she also comes tokyo drifting around corners at a ridiculous speed, giving me little time to react if I'm doing something else.
-The butcher does make noise.. sometimes. Sometimes I can hear him stomping around the house, and sometimes I can't. It could be an immersion thing, like I'm too focused on a lock or something to hear him but I don't think that's the case. He's fine, otherwise.
-Jumping up into vents is really hard and the controls for this, specifically, are confusing. I thought I'd worked out that you have to hold space but that doesn't always work, so I end up in a panic and either have to run off somewhere else or just get caught.
-Returning to volume, some sounds were REALLY LOUD and others were quiet. For example, the first time you get caught, [spoiler]removing the door pins makes an ear piercing noise that actually hurt [/spoiler], whereas other things are just weirdly quiet, including some dialogue in Night Shift. 

I reaaaally want to like this game and I'm willing to give it another shot at another point in time, but I really don't like having my time wasted. The stealth just needs so much more work. I hate that I didn't enjoy this. Maybe I'm too impatient for a horror/stealth immersion sim but being frustrated just killed the entire vibe of the game, where there was potential to really feel terrified.

Suffers from some serious problems. I have a high tolerance for difficult games. Stay Out of The House had enough bad decisions in it that I had to put it down. 

Firstly: The Visuals. I've played both games from the late 90s and games with low-res graphics which take inspiration from the era. SOTH uses this visual style, too, but it is designed in a way that makes playing the game unpleasant. Small items, even with the occasional glint, can still be easily missed. I thought I was softlocked twice because I didn't know items were there. I had the fact that the butcher holds a key spoiled for me, which I'm positive would have made me believe I was softlocked a third time if I wasn't spoiled. When stylistic decisions get in the way of the game functioning to someone who plays a lot of games, there is a large problem. Additionally, the thirstier and hungrier your character gets, the more blurry your vision becomes. Typically, obscuring vision in games for long periods of time is not a good idea.

Self-defense is difficult. Aiming the Revolver causes your character to be frozen to the ground. 

Then there is the Butcher himself. What caused me to put the game down was the fact that (at least on Hard Mode), the Butcher seems to be on a very tight leash to the player. It was rare that the Butcher wasn't in my immediate vicinity. Most frustratingly, the Butcher would camp. I would be spotted and flee to the vents, and the Butcher would turn on the gas to flush me out. The game tells you in a note that the Butcher is forgetful and will lose aggro after some time. If you emerge from the vents to turn off the gas, the Butcher will often be close by to catch you. So, I hid in the safe room for a few minutes before going out to turn off the gas. The butcher was still there. "Ok", I thought, "I'll just try again but wait even longer". I came back after fifteen whole minutes and the Butcher was still camping the exit. There is another exit from the vents, but you do not have enough oxygen to make it. I was literally trapped. There were also instances where the Butcher would spontaneously check under the bed where I was hiding even though there was no indication I was in the area. 

A small nitpick: the intro is way too long. It took me about 40 whole minutes to get to the actual game. Go the route of making there be an "Intro" button on the Main Menu so people don't have to wait to play the actual game. In addition, the Intro's first part is based on time. No matter what, each player will be sitting there waiting for something to happen.

To clarify, I've played games like this before. I've beaten all 3 Granny games (something I regret), as well as beating Amnesia: The Bunker on Hard. I very much have the capability to beat games of this type and at this difficulty, but I also don't like wasting my time. When this game is working properly, it is a good time. It is working properly around 40% of the time. 48/100 DNF

tl;dr - fairly priced game, great sound design and art direction, pacing in the prequel chapters is incredible and had me scared constantly. Unfortunately it falls apart with uninspired and silly puzzles, terrible maze-like hallways, and an oppressive antagonist that left me too visually impaired to feel like I had any hope of escaping. There's definitely something here for a niche audience that likes replaying/perfecting the gameplay loop, but it wasn't for me.

This game has amazing sound design, a very well made aesthetic, and the build up in the prequel chapters leading up to the titular "House" was very well done.

Unfortunately, once you make it to The House, the game begins to slow to a near halt. This is the main part of the game, the prequel chapters can largely be looked at as walking simulators with limited interaction.

You're in a house where a killer (or multiple killers?) stalks the hallways. You need to escape by solving puzzles and exploring and at the same time avoid this killer. Where things really fell apart for me was in how hard it was to avoid this stupid killer, and there are a few things that all come together which made me ultimately give up and abandon the game.

[b]Awareness[/b]
There is little to no warning for when the killer is nearby - I would be moving around and it was pretty much silent, and then the screen has a VHS distortion effect on it and then there's loud screaming sounds as the killer is now in front of me and stabbing or bashing me, moving after me at an incredibly fast pace. It was stunningly terrifying the first couple times, and quickly became frustrating and cheap after that. The distortion on the screen is very aggressive, and the killer is very fast... it was just so disorienting and ultimately I would always die to the killer when they found me.

[b]Level Design[/b]
Understand that this is where the one-two knock-out punch came together to have me give up on this game. The areas are very small and cramped, and winding. Lots of turns to take in this cozy little house of horrors. The game is also very dark and you have a limited inventory that is slow to navigate through AND opening the inventory menu does not pause the game. There's the inventory menu which I would like to rely on but it doesn't pause the game, so there was a button on the controller to cycle through items which was even slower but you can move while cycling so this was mainly how I worked through the inventory system.

[b]Puzzles...[/b]
Not much to say but the game is essentially an escape room with a bunch of nonsensical puzzles to wade through. I'll talk about the difficulty choices here and hopefully you understand why I put it in the section about puzzles. There were several difficulty settings, hard, normal, easy, exploration. Hard added a hunger/thirst system which I started the game on because my friends wanted me to suffer and I quite enjoy hard mode when I pick up horror games anyways (this mode was quickly dropped after 2 deaths in The House.) Normal is supposedly a standard mode without hunger/thirst and the killer has weaker awareness... but it didn't matter, because when the killer is near me the screen distorts HEAVILY with the aforementioned VHS static and my ears are lit up with screeching and screaming while the killer runs insanely fast toward me through extremely dark hallways filled with twists and turns. I never tried easy, after a few Normal mode attempts me and my friends decided "okay... maybe we should be starting on explore mode so we can at least understand the house." Bear in mind, we've literally solved nothing so far, the most I've done is pick up a granola bar, a lighter, an alarm clock, and a sound/light meter. So we played in Explore mode and through this mode we explored a large amount of the house (we made it to the backyard, which is where we finally gave up and quit.)
There isn't much to say about the puzzles, they're what you'd expect from something like this. You find a 4 digit tumbler lock and in a different area you find a piece of paper that says the answer on it, you take that item which lets you cut a wire in a different area so you can open a door to a new area and find another item to go back and get another item that lets you open another door that leads to a meat scale that you of course fill with human body parts so it explodes and a gear pops out that lets you change the time on a clock to 5 so that a hidden passageway opens on the nearby wall so you can carry on and get a new item, pretty standard horror game puzzle faire.

In the end, I was walking through a hall where the ground was pitch black with some silver/grey scratches on it, and I fell to my death (you can "die" 2 times before a gameover on the third death) because the pitch black and silver/grey ground was replaced with a slightly different looking pitch black and silver/grey hole filled with barbed wire (????) When I finally made it back to that area, I couldn't find my items I had lost, and some of them were (I assume) mission critical.

To be charitable to the game, I think there's an audience for the game. With how insanely difficult it was to hide from or avoid the killer, I think it's intended that you first play the game in explore mode. It was a hard enough game as it is just to navigate and solve the puzzles of the house without any killer breathing down (and breaking) your neck. After playing through the spooky horror house which, theoretically, shouldn't take too long to complete, you can do it all over again with the challenge of being hounded by a killer. Beyond that, you can challenge yourself further with the hard mode that makes the killer even harder to deal with AND adds survival mechanics with hunger/thirst. If this sounds appealing to you, I honestly think this game is a huge winner. Like I said at the start, the sound design is incredible, the build up to the spooks is fantastic, the art design is awesome and hits me hard in the ps1 nostalgia.

Unfortunately, I wanted something a little more compelling, and walking around a haunted house with no threats (besides the few you can walk in to, oopsie!) was very dull to me. There was also no middle ground, because even on normal mode, the killer felt oppressive and quite literally blinding.
